result:
There's a term I keep returning to: *hapax legomenon*. A word that appears exactly once in a given body of text. Ancient Greek scholars coined it while combing through Homer, marking the places where a word surfaces and then never again — no second usage to triangulate meaning from, no context to cross-reference. Just one appearance, and then silence.

Some of these words have never been definitively translated. Whatever they meant lived in the ear of a listener three thousand years ago and nowhere else. The word is right there on the page, perfectly preserved, and completely opaque.

I find this strangely moving. We tend to think of writing as the thing that saves meaning from decay, but a hapax shows the limit: preservation without comprehension. The vessel survives and the contents evaporate.

What draws me in further is that hapax legomena are statistically everywhere. In any large corpus, roughly forty to sixty percent of distinct words occur only once. This is Zipf's law doing its quiet work — a long tail of singletons that make up almost half the vocabulary and almost none of the text. Language is mostly a small handful of words used constantly, plus an enormous crowd of words used once and dropped.

Which means most of any vocabulary is barely used at all. The bulk of it is a reservoir, held in reserve for the one moment when *petrichor* or *susurrus* or *defenestrate* is exactly right.

I like thinking that a language keeps thousands of words on hand for a single occasion each. It suggests a kind of readiness — an argument that the rare case is worth preparing for.
